industryMedical.title: AI adoption for medical institutions, starting with organizing records and preparing documents.

lead.p: Say you want to try using AI to draft referral letters.

The information you need is in the electronic medical record. You have the format you always use. But where will patient information be handled, and how will it get into that format? Once you think it through to the point where a doctor checks the content, it is not something you can decide to adopt right away.

Nursing summaries at discharge or transfer, handled by the nursing department. Medication management summaries, prepared by the pharmacy department to hand over to other hospitals and pharmacies. For documents like these too, we work out with you a flow in which records are gathered, put into the format, and checked by the professional in charge.
Hospital directors and management are of course welcome to consult us, as are directors of nursing, nurse managers, directors of pharmacy, and staff in IT and administrative departments.

Cor. helps from the very first step: looking into your current data and the way work is done. Which tasks to reduce, and which judgments stay with people. From sorting that out to designing and implementing the setup, we move forward together.

Initial registration date: November 7, 2026. Registration number: JP26/00000364.

founder.h2: Using AI to create an environment where people can focus on the decisions people should make.

body.p: Diagnosis affects patients' lives. I believe that glibly “making everything more efficient with AI” goes against what this is really meant to be about.

body.strong: Use AI to create an environment where people can focus on the decisions people should make.

body.p: That, I believe, is the essence of AI systems for healthcare.

Gathering and organizing the information recorded in past medical charts: using AI to assist with that work is something we can consider. Diagnosis, on the other hand, is the doctor's job. Nursing judgments and pharmaceutical assessments, too, belong to the respective professionals. I want to draw that line clearly.

We start with administrative and routine tasks. Systems that go into diagnosis or treatment are something I want to consider after that, based on the necessary checks of laws and regulations and of safety.

sections.h2: Referral letters, nursing summaries, medication management summaries. We start from the formats you actually use.

sections.h3: Doctors and clinical departments: drafting referral letters in your own hospital's format

sections.p: Even when a summary for the referral letter can be produced, the work of transferring it into the usual format remains. An interview with a clinic director published by medimo, a provider of AI for healthcare, also describes this work.

Cor. checks where the necessary records are and how they can be extracted from the electronic medical record. We also look into the export and integration methods the vendor provides, and the extent to which they can be used.

Information is gathered and put into the format, and the doctor checks it against the original records, then corrects and finalizes it. We consider feasible ways to do this, including a system used through a browser on in-hospital terminals.

sections.h3: Nursing department: preparing nursing summaries for discharge or transfer

sections.p: For example, looking back over the course of care so far and summarizing what to hand over to the next facility.
Even if AI can produce a draft, you still need to decide which records to use, how to check it against the original records, and who reviews and finalizes it.

Cor. talks with directors of nursing, nurse managers and the people who actually write the records, to understand your current formats and workflow. We consider the time spent writing together with the effort needed to check and correct.

A collection of nursing DX case studies from the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) also presents a case in which the director of nursing, ward nurse managers and others worked out the workflow, and nurses check AI drafts against the original records.

sections.h3: Pharmacy department: preparing medication management summaries and in-hospital materials

sections.p: Handing over the necessary information to the next medical institution or community pharmacy: the Japanese Society of Hospital Pharmacists publishes the medication management summary as a form for that purpose.
Which records go into which form? Cor. looks into where we can support the work: gathering information, transcribing it, or drafting.

Researching drug information and preparing materials to share within the hospital can also be part of the investigation. We think about a form in which the source documents and update dates can be checked, while reviewing the content and making pharmaceutical judgments remain with pharmacists.

Who is in charge, which formats are used, who checks and finalizes. Once we understand how each department differs, we decide how much to leave to AI. For transcribing into fixed fields and formatting, we also compare existing functions and rule-based processing.

sections.h2: Where patient information is handled, by whom, and how.

sections.p: Before Cor. receives any real data, we sign a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) and agree on the information to be used and where the work will be done.

Who is given access? What work is it used for? Where is it stored, and when is it returned or deleted? We sort this out together with the hospital's own rules. The scope of AI processing, how records are handled, and the role of the people who check are also decided at the design stage.

For each individual build, we follow the MHLW's security management guidelines and the hospital's own operations, and check everything down to permissions, equipment updates, and backup and recovery methods.

sections.h3: We first check whether your data really needs a “big move”

sections.p: Gathering your existing data into a new place so that you can use AI: that preparation could become the very reason adoption stalls.

Cor. also looks into options that make use of where the data is kept now. Will you use the existing shared drive, make use of an in-hospital server, or set up something new? We consider where data is stored separately from where AI processes it.

A setup that processes patient information without sending it outside the hospital can also be considered. The setup that can actually be built depends on how it connects to the electronic medical record, the functions needed and the hospital's operations.

sections.h3: Before buying equipment, we check what will be used and how much

sections.p: Cor. has the technology to build a local LLM into systems on consumer PCs. A local LLM is generative AI that runs on your own PCs, in-hospital servers or similar hardware.

We check the amount of data, the number of people using it at the same time, and the response speed needed, and work out the setup. As part of that, we judge whether your current equipment can be used or whether more needs to be prepared.

We learn the terminology, formats and practices of clinical work by asking the people who actually do that work. Cor. takes charge of everything from infrastructure and data foundations to sorting out requirements and development, and gives the system shape together with the people who know the work.

sections.h2: Turning even a single department's request into a build plan the hospital can evaluate.

sections.p: Even when the nursing or pharmacy department starts the discussion, we identify who will actually use the system, who reviews systems and information management, and who decides on budget and contracts. We proceed with the people who need to be involved, in line with how your facility is organized.

sections.h3: At the first meeting, we hear what you want to do and what is holding it up

sections.p: The meeting is planned to take about one hour. We ask what you want to do, what is already under way, and what difficulties you face in moving forward.
We sort out what is essential and what you would like to have if possible, and present a rough plan of what to look into next.

sections.h3: We look into your data and work within the agreed scope

sections.p: If you are satisfied with the direction, we move on to an NDA and a contract for the investigation.
Through interviews with the people involved and other means, we find out who uses which records, for what purpose and how often. Where needed, we also discuss site visits.

sections.h3: We compare build plans and decide what to implement

sections.p: When there are several options, we present them in a form that is easy to compare within the hospital, from a bare-minimum setup to one that covers the whole. If something is hard to achieve, we tell you frankly.

If we judge that it can be implemented in a short time, we can also consider a contract that covers both the investigation and building an MVP, after confirming cost and scope. An MVP is a system with the minimum features needed.

Uses involving diagnosis or treatment need to be checked, depending on their intended purpose and risk, for matters such as whether they count as a medical device under the Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Act (PMD Act). The policy that professionals check and decide, and the system's legal status, are confirmed separately.

sections.h2: In an age when AI is a given, what is the role of people?

sections.p: Deciding what to automate is also deciding where people put their energy.

Doctors, nurses, pharmacists. Letting each of them focus on professional judgment and on their interactions with patients. To that end, how can we support the work of finding records, organizing them and turning them into documents? That is where Cor. wants to start thinking with you.
If we are going to build a system, we want it to be used on the ground for a long time. So please talk to us, even before your ideas have come together.

industryShigyo.title: Building AI into the work of licensed professional firms, while checking the grounds for each answer.

lead.p: Say a client sends you a question similar to one you have handled before.

You found the past answer. But you can't tell what was checked to reach that conclusion. Even if you have AI draft an answer, you end up searching for the supporting documents all over again from scratch.
Cor. looks into where your documents are kept and how checks are done, and designs with you a way to produce draft answers whose grounds can be traced.
We break down your usual work and bring AI in little by little, starting with the tasks where it helps. While keeping the burden on day-to-day work low, we build a system that suits your firm.

Heads and partners of licensed professional firms (tax accountants, lawyers, labor and social security attorneys and others), as well as the staff in charge of adoption at those firms, are welcome to consult us.

sections.h2: Making it possible to go back to the documents to check, right alongside the draft answer.

sections.p: Which document, kept where, is the answer based on?
Not just a list of document names, but which part of the answer refers to which passage of the original document. The design includes presenting this in a way your staff can cross-check.

ul: Where the document is kept, and how to access the original file.
The passage in the source that corresponds to the draft answer.
Information needed for checking, such as the client or matter, and the point in time the document reflects.

sections.p: Whether that document can be applied to the question at hand is for a professional to judge. Showing a reference is not the same as the answer being correct.
That is exactly why we also design the flow of going back to the original documents, checking the content and finalizing it.

sections.h3: Tax accountant firms: preparing draft answers for clients together with the documents to check them against

sections.p: Searching past consultation records and in-house materials, then drafting an answer: starting from tasks like these, we consider how far we can support you.
The published policy of Tsuji & Hongo Tax & Consulting (辻・本郷税理士法人) also lists preparing documents and assisting with answers to routine questions as uses of generative AI.

In the investigation with Cor., we sort out the clients and fiscal years in scope, the documents to refer to, and who checks the content. Tax judgments are made by tax accountants; we support the work of gathering the information those judgments need.

sections.h3: Law firms: linking the organizing of case materials with checking the original text

sections.p: Finding the materials received from the client and organizing the sequence of events. We design a flow that lets you go from that draft back to the original text you want to check.
Bengo Kakumei (弁護革命), a tool for legal practice, has also published features for summarizing documents, building chronologies, and opening the referenced passage from the output.

Cor. also checks which parts existing tools can handle, and considers how to connect them to your firm's materials and practice. Legal assessment and how matters are explained to the client remain with the lawyers.

sections.h3: Labor and social security attorney firms: organizing in-house FAQs and client-specific information

sections.p: Finding the manual shared within the firm. Checking the answer given to an earlier labor consultation. Then confirming whether it fits the current client's situation.
Fukuoka Social Insurance and Labor Consultants Corporation (福岡社会保険労務士法人) has published how it builds up FAQs and manuals into a system its staff can search.

Cor. distinguishes knowledge used in common from client-specific materials, and designs a setup in which the necessary information can be checked. Labor judgments are made by labor and social security attorneys; together with you, we also sort out the flow in which staff gather information and ask for it to be checked.

sections.h2: So that preparing for adoption doesn't bring your everyday work to a halt.

body.p: Switching the work people do now to an AI-centered way of working all at once. If you try to change everything together, from organizing and migrating documents to the way work is done, the preparation itself can become a major job.

What I want to do first is break down the work as it is now. Find, task by small task, where handing it to AI would help. Keep the extra effort added to everyday work as low as possible, and save labor little by little.
Not changing everything in one go, but seeing things from the client's everyday point of view. That's why I want to start by listening to each firm, one at a time.

industryConstruction.title: Less re-keying of daily construction reports. Connecting the information you already have to each prime contractor's formats.

lead.p: Say a daily report entered on a smartphone at the site has reached the office.
The same content has to be written out again in the Excel file for the prime contractor. For another prime contractor's project, it has to fit yet another format.
The data has been entered into the app. Even so, the paperwork isn't finished.

Cor. works with you to build a system that uses AI and conventional programs to reduce that re-keying and reformatting. It takes the information available from your existing apps and drafts documents in the format each recipient needs. We design the whole flow around the work on site, through to a person checking and approving the content.

At construction companies and specialty contractors that work with several prime contractors, presidents, heads of construction departments, and the office and adoption staff who support the sites are welcome to consult us.

sections.h2: Reducing the burden on the people who receive your existing apps' output.

sections.p: Each prime contractor uses a different system, so entering the same information more than once becomes a burden. This problem is also described in guidelines from the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (MLIT).
What Cor. looks at first is how people handle the information after it comes out of the app.

sections.strong: “Instead of changing the existing app, reduce the burden on the people who receive its output.”

sections.p: Starting over by modifying the app itself every time the prime contractor or project changes: with that approach, the adjustments keep going, and the road to actually using it can become a long detour. We want to avoid ending up with something that is tested over and over but not used on site.
First, we make use of the features your current software already offers. Some construction management products include form generation and integration with external systems.

Then: which information is being copied into which documents? We check which parts existing export and integration features can cover, and which parts still need human work. This is also where we confirm the range of data available, the output formats, and the permissions and contract terms.
We aim for a setup that, even when new prime contractors or formats are added, lets you sort out what can be shared across them and what needs extra handling.

sections.h2: Putting “this form is the only one that's different here” into words, together.

sections.p: The people who can prepare these documents also know things that aren't written on the forms.

For example, the same information goes into different fields, or is summarized differently, depending on where it is submitted. On the usual form they can fill it in without hesitation, but for an exceptional form they check other documents.
If those judgments exist only in the head of the person in charge, just matching how the forms look won't produce a system that fits day-to-day work.
First, please let us work with you to put into words the “tacit knowledge” that only the staff at that site know.

sections.h2: From the smartphone at the site to the documents at the office.

sections.p: For example, photos taken on a smartphone, or work records entered into an app. If someone has to find them again on an office PC and retype them into another format, we start by reviewing that hand-off.

Tasks done on the smartphone are made easy to enter and check on the spot. The information captured there is passed automatically to the office PC or a shared location and used to draft the documents needed. We consider systems like this while checking your current apps' export and integration features and terms of use.
Features that link information recorded on a smartphone to construction management software and use it to generate forms are already offered by existing products.

Where needed, we provide review screens and AI chat screens that can be used from a smartphone or PC. We aim to let the site and the office each keep working on the devices that suit them, while reducing the hassle of switching devices and entering things twice.

sections.h3: Support for transcription and drafting, with checking and approval left to people.

sections.p: Cor. designs the system so that the steps of checking a document's content, finalizing it and submitting it keep a review and approval by the person your company designates.
Where the original information is missing or inconsistent, it is treated as an item that needs confirmation. We place importance on not turning what AI has guessed directly into a finalized record.

For transcription and tallying where the form's fields are fixed, we also compare handling them with ordinary programs. Following how the work is actually done, we divide it into parts where text is organized, parts handled by fixed rules, and parts where people decide.

sections.h2: Making use of the devices and software you have, and adding as little as possible.

sections.p: Smartphones, feature phones, tablets, PCs. We start by making as much use as possible of the equipment and software already at your sites.

If you use feature phones, we check the models, network conditions and the conditions under which they can safely stay in use, and consider what role they can keep in your current communication and record-keeping.

sections.strong: Aim for the greatest effect with the smallest additions.

sections.p: Before adding new devices or apps, we check with you what is in use now and where people are passing information on again by hand.

The devices people operate and the place where AI runs are each chosen to fit the work. For example, a setup in which smartphones are used on site and AI processing happens on PCs or servers in your office. Cor. handles everything from infrastructure and data foundations to sorting out requirements and development, including building a local LLM into consumer PCs.
The equipment and connection methods needed are decided based on the information handled, the number of users, the processing speed required, and network conditions at the site.

Before handling any real data, we sign a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) and agree on the information to be used and where the work will be done. For information received from prime contractors or partner companies too, we confirm how far it may be used.
Including whether to use local or cloud, we sort out where data is stored and processed, who can view it, how usage is logged, and how backups and deletion are handled.

sections.h2: We start by looking at the documents you use most.

sections.p: The first meeting is planned to take about one hour. We ask what you want to do, what is already under way and what is holding you back right now, and present a rough plan of what to look into next.

If you are satisfied with the direction, we move on to an NDA and a contract for the investigation. We first look at the documents you use most and the forms that are exceptions, and decide the scope to tackle first.

After the investigation, we propose the preparation needed and a build plan. Start with a minimal setup, or also cover related tasks? If there are options, we lay them out for comparison, and if something is hard to achieve, we tell you frankly.
If we judge that it can be implemented in a short time, we can also consider combining the investigation with building a system with the minimum features needed, after confirming cost and scope.
We don't stop once it is built. Together we check whether the re-keying effort has gone down, whether things are easy to check, and whether the input and preparation burden on site has grown.

founder.h2: Improvements that get people saying, “We finished five minutes earlier than last month.”

body.p: What I'm aiming for is automation that people keep using for a long time in their daily work.

If you suddenly change the workflow, people have to relearn how to operate things, and manuals have to be written. The everyday work is hard enough already, and now there's even more preparation on top. If the people on site can't keep up and the system ends up unused, that defeats the whole purpose.
So: little by little, every week, every month, at a pace that doesn't strain anyone. Tasks get simpler, and work finishes just a little earlier. I want to value that steady build-up.

body.strong: “We finished five minutes earlier than last month.”
“What should we change next month to make it even easier?”

body.p: I want the staff on site to be saying things like that.
Unglamorous, but steadily moving forward. Leaving everyday routines unchanged, in a good way, while things quietly get better.
That's the kind of system I want to build together with our clients.

lead.p: Say a piece of equipment isn't running right.
A veteran listens to the sound, looks closely at the work in front of them, and checks the spot that is different from usual. What remains in the record afterward is a single phrase: “Part replaced.”
What did they look at, and how did they decide? Are those clues being passed on to the next person in charge?

Cor. combines images, video, audio and existing records to put shop-floor knowledge into a form AI can work with. From how to collect the information needed to a system the next person can refer to while working, we design and implement it with you.

Presidents of manufacturing companies, plant managers, and people in production engineering, maintenance and other roles who want to advance skills transfer or the use of AI on the shop floor are welcome to consult us.

sections.h2: Down to the clues behind judgments that never make it into the daily report.

sections.p: The order of the steps may be recorded, but differences in sound, the feel of things, when to check, and the reason behind a judgment are not. How do you pass that kind of knowledge on?

A survey of manufacturers by JILPT (the Japan Institute for Labour Policy and Training) also lists, among the reasons skills transfer does not go well, a lack of time to spare and a lack of communication between those who teach and those who learn.
The starting point, as Cor. sees it, is finding out what, if kept during everyday work, would help the next person.

For example, record a single inspection or adjustment. Watch the footage with an experienced worker and briefly ask, “What were you checking here?” Compare it with existing daily reports and equipment records, and narrow down the clues worth keeping.

sections.h2: Gathering information from the shop floor, in addition to input on PCs and smartphones.

sections.p: Work that takes both hands. Moments when you can't easily step away from the equipment. Tasks where subtle changes are hard to describe once you write them up afterward.
In situations like these, we start by thinking about a way of capturing information that suits the site.

Cor. has worked with manufacturers of smart devices in Japan and abroad to develop software that captures information from the field. Besides PCs and smartphones, we treat smart glasses, smart cameras, smartwatches and similar devices as options depending on the use.

sections.h3: We are still developing together with a smart glasses manufacturer today.

sections.p: We are currently working with the manufacturer to develop smart glasses that read text and convey it by voice for people with visual impairments.

What we deal with in this development, too, is the chain from receiving information from the field, to processing it with AI, to returning it to the user. We will apply that experience to designing systems that gather and make use of the information needed on the factory floor.

sections.h3: We choose the equipment based on the information you want to keep.

sections.p: Smart glasses if you need footage close to the worker's line of sight. A camera to watch hand movements and what is happening around them. Video or time-lapse to look back over the flow of work. We consider methods like these together with your existing equipment, devices and software.

Who will use it, and where? Will it get in the way of the work? Can it capture the changes that matter? We check all this, including noise and network conditions on site, and choose what equipment to add.

A skills-transfer case from Hitachi and Daikin also describes how measuring with many instruments alone did not reveal the difference from skilled workers, and how interviews with skilled workers were used to decide what to observe and to narrow down the measurement methods.

sections.h2: Passing it to AI, “interpreted so it understands.”

sections.p: What Cor. wants to be is the bridge between the shop floor, AI, and the people who take on the work next.

Linking the footage and sound collected to which equipment, under what conditions, and what is being done in that scene. Making the reasons an experienced worker gave for a judgment checkable from the corresponding scene.

sections.strong: Collect the data AI needs, and pass it to AI “interpreted so it understands.”

sections.p: NEDO, too, names the fact that the meaning of in-company data and the relationships among it are not organized as a challenge for using AI, and treats preparing such data into a usable state, and evaluating it, as a subject of research.

sections.p: How something felt to the touch, or why things were checked in that order, cannot always be understood from footage alone. We take care not to record a reason AI has guessed as if it were a fact about how the person judged.

sections.h2: All the way to the next person being able to use it when it is needed.

sections.p: For example, searching for related records by equipment name or by a symptom someone noticed, and being able to view the confirmed explanation together with the scene in the original footage. Systems like this are something we can consider.

Do people want to view it on a device on the floor, or review it with a mentor after the work? We decide the screens and how information is returned based on where it is used and by whom. The devices people operate and the place where AI processing happens are also designed to fit their respective conditions.

We separate the parts that existing search and record management can cover, the parts AI organizes and analyzes, and the parts people check. How to organize the recorded footage, and whether additional training of a model is needed, are also decided by looking at the goals and the data.

Even if similar records exist from the past, the equipment and conditions are not necessarily the same this time. We design it so that the actual response and the operation of equipment are decided according to your company's procedures and lines of responsibility.

Whether the knowledge has been passed on is checked by whether the next person can reach the information they need and understand the clues behind the judgment. Taking into account the burden on those who record and the time mentors spend checking, we keep adjusting it into a form that can be sustained.

lead.p: Six months left until the teacher's retirement. We did not learn this until our first visit to the school after the contract was signed.

founder.h2: I, too, had overlooked the possibility that things had not been properly aligned.

body.p: This happened some time ago, when Cor. was commissioned by a prime contractor and took part in developing a system for the teachers, staff and students of a vocational school.

On our first visit after the contract was signed, I heard that the teacher who ran the school's internal database would reach retirement age and retire in six months. Nothing had been done to prepare for it, and if things stayed as they were, the running of the school itself could run into problems.

Information such as students, courses and timetables was kept in an internal database that had been in use for many years. The teacher entered data into it directly, while other teachers and administrative staff, to make up for how hard it was to use, kept their own separate records in Access or FileMaker.
Between the prime contractor and the school, requirements definition and alignment had not progressed far enough. And I, too, had overlooked that possibility.

From there, the implementation plan changed again and again. We started by putting the data foundation in order, and on this project spent about six months consolidating the data into a database on Google Cloud.
The system people talk about wanting to build and what is really needed on the ground may not line up. Not checking that enough was also my own failing.

Because of this experience, at Cor. we want to start by looking into and sorting out the current situation together with you, even when the consultation is about AI that uses a school's internal data.

sections.p: What can be built is not always what the work on the ground calls for. We add features and take them away. We separate what to leave to AI from what to handle with fixed rules or existing functions.

sections.h2: We think about equipment after confirming the work you want to do.

sections.p: Cor. has the technology to build a local LLM (generative AI that runs on your own PC or similar hardware) into systems on consumer PCs. We can handle everything end to end, from infrastructure and data foundations to sorting out requirements and development.

We check the work involved, the amount of data and the number of people using it at the same time, and consider the setup you need. As part of that, we also consider whether your current equipment can be used or whether more needs to be prepared. Even when it runs on campus, we check permissions, external communication and storage locations against the school's rules.

Terada also has experience selling online advertising at Recruit. Listening to wishes that have not yet taken shape and turning them into concrete actions: that experience also feeds into how we run consultations.

We learn the terminology and practices specific to your school by asking your teachers and staff. The people who know the work and Cor., in charge of technology and data foundations, aim for the same goal.

sections.h2: From investigation to a build plan and implementation.

sections.h3: We decide what will be shared and where the work will be done

sections.p: If the first meeting leaves you satisfied with the direction, we move on to a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) and a contract for the investigation. Actual data is shared only after the NDA is signed and we have agreed on what may be shared and used, and where it will be handled.

We decide where to work from among the school's Google Drive, OneDrive or local environment, or an environment on Cor.'s side that we have agreed on. We also discuss how to proceed from the second meeting onward, including site visits.

sections.h3: We look into where the data is and how it is actually used

sections.p: We take stock of the data that can be used this time and, where needed, interview or survey teachers, staff and others involved. Who uses it, when, where, for what and how? We also check how often and how much it is used.
We compare options such as moving the data and using it where it is now.

sections.h3: We propose a build plan that suits your school

sections.p: When there are several options, we present them in tiers (for example, good / better / best), from a full setup to a minimal one. We use whatever format is easiest for the school, such as Google Docs or Word documents. If the options are limited, or something is hard to achieve, we tell you frankly.

If we can judge at the first meeting that a short implementation is feasible, we can also consider a contract that covers both the investigation and building an MVP (a system with the minimum features needed), after confirming the additional cost and scope. In that case, we discuss delivering a working MVP in place of a minimal-setup plan.

The role Cor. wants to play is something like a life planner and development company for your AI project, rolled into one. If we are going to build a system, we want it to be used on the ground for a long time. So please let us think it through with you, even before anything has taken shape.

aboutPage.founderStoryHeading: Turns out, I was the alien
founderStoryExcerpt: In kindergarten, I couldn't join in the group dances. When they sent me outside, I rode a tricycle around and around the yard.
At my elementary school entrance ceremony, I chased a butterfly that flew past me, right out of the gym.
Once, wanting to know whether a magnifying glass could really start a fire, I held one over a pile of fallen leaves for the whole lunch break. It started a small fire.
In my head, all of it made sense. I wanted to do something, and I went at it the fastest way I knew. But to everyone else, I must have been a kid who might do anything.
By fourth grade, no one invited me to play anymore.

So I devoured books on behavioral psychology at the library. Where people look, how they move, when they pause. Ways to read, from the outside, the feelings people don't put into words. By sixth grade, I was even trusted to be class president.
But I was always exhausted. Reading faces, choosing words that wouldn't spoil the mood. Talking that way, conversations ended without what I really thought ever getting across.
Wasn't there a more natural way for feelings to get through? I had been asking that since I was a child.

questions.question: What is the first step in introducing AI?
questions.answer: The first decision is not which AI model to use. It is clarifying which data can be processed, which requires anonymization, and which must be kept in-house or in a local LLM. At Cor.Inc., we design input boundaries, permissions, logs, human approvals, and operational responsibilities first.

questions.question: How do you choose between Cloud AI and Local LLM?
questions.answer: Cloud AI is ideal for public data or general writing. However, for sensitive documents like contracts, customer logs, and internal knowledge, we consider secure in-house environments or Local LLMs. Rather than dismissing Cloud AI, we utilize both based on data confidentiality and requirements.

questions.question: What does the Confidential Data AI Assessment include?
questions.answer: We conduct workflow interviews, inventory tasks for AI adaptation, classify data, separate cloud vs. local processing, analyze security risks, and draft a PoC strategy. The estimated cost is ¥100k - ¥300k.

Our quotes make the assumptions, risks, and scope of work clear.

questions.question: How are security and privacy handled?
questions.answer: We build practical requirements into the design: input data management, access rights, operation logs, human approval flows, deletion rules, and clear operational responsibility. Internally, we operate an ISMS and completed the Stage 2 audit for ISO/IEC 27001 in October 2026. We expect certification registration around December 2026.

questions.question: What is Grift?
questions.answer: Grift is our own product that extracts verifiable facts from an engineer's development record (git history). It assigns no scores or rankings and uses no AI (LLM) for measurement, so it gives the same result no matter who runs it, and whoever receives the output can verify it. Only when the person has named their own identity and a consent record exists does the report open with short sentences in Japanese on how that person's recorded work was done and with questions worth asking in an interview. The sentences themselves are not checked by verification; what can be verified are the numbers behind them. The CLI is published free of charge as open source under the MIT License, and we are accepting inquiries about trials (PoCs) that help sales teams at recruiting agencies and SES (IT staffing) companies explain why they recommend a candidate, backed by evidence, and help hiring teams at companies that build their own software see, from the records a candidate chooses to share, what their work has actually involved.

sections.title: 6. Security Control Measures

For Specific Personal Information, access privileges are configured so that only the personnel in charge of the relevant affairs can access it.
Encryption: Disk encryption (FileVault) is enabled on business devices, and communications are encrypted using TLS or the like. Encryption at rest is enabled for data stored in the cloud.

Disposal: Personal data that is no longer needed is disposed of by a method that renders it irrecoverable.

Understanding the external environment: The Company uses cloud services and other services provided by U.S. businesses, and personal data may be handled in the United States. In addition, the generative AI service used for the AI Reception (Section 9 (3)) is used with a setting that does not restrict the processing location to Japan, so the country where processing takes place cannot be identified. bodyAfter: (4) Information sent to generative AI and masking: Only the content of your consultation, the AI's responses, and the information in (1)(ii) (excluding UTM parameters) are sent to the generative AI service; the information in (1)(iii) is not sent. (5) Storage and retention periods: The Company does not store the conversation sent from your browser in its original form; it stores it as a conversation excerpt that has undergone the masking in (4) and is limited in length both per message and in total. In addition, the Company stores the summary generated by the AI, organized items such as the type and stage of your consultation, and the information in (1)(iii); the conversation excerpt and the information in (1)(iii) are stored in encrypted form. These are automatically deleted after the following periods have elapsed: (i) information on your use of the AI Reception (conversation excerpt, summary, organized items, etc.): 30 days from the last exchange; (ii) information submitted at the handover step (the information in (1)(iii), together with the summary, conversation excerpt, information indicating the source of your visit, etc. stored with it): 90 days from receipt.

However, notification emails received by the Company's staff and subsequent correspondence with you are not subject to the automatic deletion above; they are handled within the scope of the purposes of use in Section 2 (1) and are disposed of in accordance with Section 6 once they are no longer needed. In addition, the outsourcing contractors in (3) may also retain information for a certain period, as specified by each business, for purposes such as providing their services and preventing misuse.

(6) Handling overseas: Of the businesses in (3), Anthropic, Resend and Cloudflare are U.S. businesses (including their affiliates), and the Company handles the provision of data to them appropriately by the methods set out in Section 4 (Use of Cloud Services and Provision to Third Parties Located Overseas). security.title: Security
security.lead: Cor. Inc. is building out its information security program to balance the speed of AI development with the responsibility of protecting our customers' valuable information. While maintaining a local-first environment where developers can be highly productive, we operate a combination of sensitivity-based access controls, approved AI tools, minimal security logging, and an incident response framework.

basicPolicy.title: Information Security Basic Policy
basicPolicy.note: The Japanese version is the authoritative text. This English translation is provided for convenience.
preamble: Cor. Inc. (hereinafter, “the Company”), under its management philosophy of “shaping the future and realizing a happy society through co-creation rather than competition,” engages in businesses including contracted AI development and AI adoption support, AI advisory and training, the provision of the AI evaluation platform “Grift,” and support for highly confidential AI operations using local LLMs.

The scope of this Basic Policy covers all operations related to the entirety of the Company's business at its head office (Fukuoka) — the planning, requirements definition, development, and operation of AI solutions, together with the associated accounting and finance work — as well as the information assets handled in those operations.

Because these businesses involve handling many information assets — including confidential information, source code, and training data entrusted to us by customers — the Company recognizes ensuring information security as a critical management issue. The Company believes that implementing appropriate safeguards for customer information collected through its operations and for the information assets it handles, and maintaining their confidentiality, integrity, and availability, forms the foundation of the trust it builds with customers and of the sustainable development of its business.

Through the establishment and operation of an information security management system (ISMS), the Company aims to prevent security incidents such as information leaks and tampering, and to that end establishes the following information security guidelines.
guidelines: The Company will identify information asset risks using defined procedures and implement appropriate risk treatment in order to establish and continually improve its information security management system.
The Company will clearly define roles and responsibilities for information security and appropriately manage its information assets.
The Company will conduct education and awareness activities for management, employees, and all related parties so that they recognize their responsibility to maintain information security.

The Company will monitor and record the implementation of its information security management system, and will improve operational reliability and pursue continual improvement through the setting and achievement of information security objectives and through periodic internal audits and management reviews.
In the unlikely event of an information security problem, the Company will immediately investigate the cause, minimize the damage, and strive to ensure business continuity.
The Company will comply with laws and regulations, other social norms, and contracts with customers concerning information assets and their handling.
The Company will consider climate change and other changes in the business environment as issues relevant to information security and business continuity.

pillars.title: Local-First
pillars.description: We use high-spec, company-issued Macs as the baseline so developers can work comfortably in a local development environment. By combining device encryption, MDM, account management, and necessary security configurations, we aim to balance development speed with information management.

pillars.title: Minimal Security Logging, Detection, and Response
pillars.description: Rather than preventively prohibiting everything, we maintain security visibility to the extent needed for our work and build a framework that can quickly detect and respond when issues arise. The data we collect is limited to work-related security telemetry, and our policy is not to excessively collect private content.

pillars.title: Sensitivity Tiers
pillars.description: Depending on the sensitivity of the information handled, we selectively use company accounts, approved AI tools, access controls, and isolated environments when needed. For non-confidential verification we prioritize speed, while applying stricter handling when dealing with customer confidential data, personal information, source code, and the like.

status.legal: Since June 2026, in collaboration with our retained legal counsel, we have been building a legal review framework covering contracts, personal information, AI use, and information security operations.
status.isms: We operate an Information Security Management System (ISMS) and are undergoing certification audits for the international standard ISO/IEC 27001. We completed the Stage 2 audit in October 2026 and expect certification registration around December 2026. Through continuous strengthening of our framework, we fulfill our responsibility to protect our customers' information.

security.aiDescription: Cor. actively leverages AI tools for our work. At the same time, when handling customer confidential data, personal information, source code, training data, and the like, we use AI tools under contracts and configurations that prevent training use, company accounts, or approved environments. AI outputs are verified by people and used only after confirming rights, accuracy, and safety.
